# Implementation {#implementation}

\ChapFrame[Implementation][bhtyellow]

This chapter presents the practical implementation of the methods and workflows developed for automated page identification and information extraction in financial documents. It describes the environments in which our experiments are conducted, the software packages used and the datasets created for benchmarking and evaluation.

Details of the ground truth creation process are provided, including annotation strategies and dataset composition. The data processing workflow is illustrated, highlighting both the experimental setup on the Datexis Kubernetes cluster and the local environment used for evaluation and reporting.

By documenting the technical decisions and solutions adopted, this chapter offers a comprehensive overview of how the proposed methodology was translated into a functional system. We hope this will facilitate reproducibility and serve as a reference for future work. We especially recommend using open-source scientific and technical publishing systems like *R Markdown* and *Quarto* to create documents that are directly linked to the data and code used for analysis.

## Environments

All computations for this thesis are conducted in two distinct environments. Tasks that do not require a \acrfull{GPU} are executed locally; the specifications of the local device are provided in Appendix \@ref(local-machine). Tasks necessitating a \acr{GPU} are performed on the [Datexis](https://prof.bht-berlin.de/loeser) Kubernetes cluster.

We also perform prototyping for most tasks on the cluster. For this purpose, an interactive docker image with \acrfull{SSH} capabilities and Python was created based on the \acrfull{vllm} docker image. In rare cases, a \acr{vllm} server is deployed on the cluster and queried from the local machine.

The experiments use the same images as the prototyping environment and connect to a persistent volume where the scripts to run and data to use are located. Results are saved on the persistent volume as well. We use 5 TB of persistent storage, most of which is occupied by cached \acrfull{LLM} safetensors.

We back up the folder containing the scripts and data to process and download the results via \acr{SSH} protocol. We use *git* for version control but do not synchronize the data from the persistent volume with GitHub. Within the local environment, we use *git* as well. All data stored locally is synchronized to a *GitHub* repository except for the 10 GB of \acrfull{json} formatted raw results.

## Software Packages

::: paragraph-start
##### Python

We use \acr{vllm} and *chromadb* to set up our in-context learning pipeline. \acr{vllm} is a fast and easy-to-use framework for providing \acr{LLM}s locally or as a service. *chromadb* is a vector database and a key component of our naive \acrfull{RAG} architecture [@gaoRetrievalAugmentedGenerationLarge2024]. It supplies the \acr{LLM}s with examples that are most similar in terms of their vector representations.
:::

For data wrangling we use *pandas*. We save our experiments results using the *json* library. We extract texts from \acrfull{PDF}s mainly with *pypdfium2* and use *sklearn* for building \acrfull{RF} classifiers.

::: paragraph-start
##### R

We use the *tidyverse* library for data wrangling and to create our visualizations with *ggplot*. We use *h2o* for building \acr{RF} models on the Datexis cluster and *shapviz* to interpret these models. *knitr* is used to create this thesis document.
:::

## Ground Truth Datasets

### Ground Truth Creation

This section provides a detailed account of the ground truth creation process, including our initial annotation strategy and subsequent improvements informed by later iterations and experimental findings.

::: paragraph-start
##### Page Identification

We identify target pages in the selected documents using the search function, the \acrfull{TOC} or by manually scrolling through all pages. For each target page, the file path, page number and type are recorded in a \acrfull{csv} file. In some reports, multiple pages correspond to a single target type; in these cases, all relevant pages are included in the ground truth. Occasionally, the **Aktiva** and **Passiva** tables appear on the same page, resulting in a single entry labeled *Aktiva&Passiva*. If a table spans two pages, both are documented. In total, we created 252 entries, excluding pages requiring \acrfull{OCR} processing.
:::

To ensure correctness, all identified pages are extracted from their original PDF files and compiled into a single document. This process helps resolve discrepancies between the page numbers displayed in the PDF viewer and the actual file page numbers. We also review pages classified as targets by multiple models in initial experiments, which allows us to identify additional target tables spanning two pages.

In an earlier sample, we catalogued all pages containing any type of table. This subset includes all pages classified as containing **Aktiva**, **Passiva** or **GuV** tables using the \acrfull{regex} approach, encompassing both true and false positives. This ground truth supports the evaluation of various Python libraries, \acr{LLM}s and visual models for table detection. Results are presented in the Appendix \@ref(table-detection-benchmark).

::: paragraph-start
##### Information Extraction

Numeric values are manually transcribed from the annual reports into \acr{csv} files, with thousands separators and decimal delimiters standardized. Values are multiplied by 1_000 if the corresponding column specifies a currency unit. The \acr{csv} files are prefilled with all entities defined in the legal text, identified by their complete hierarchy.
:::

Occasionally, a single line in the legal text is split into multiple lines in the annual reports. In such cases, the sum is entered into the most appropriate row in the \acr{csv} file. Entities that do not match any in the legal text are omitted. In the first iteration, the \acr{csv} files are not prefilled with numeric values.

In the second iteration, the \acr{csv} files include predictions from Qwen3-235B. We review these values, highlight errors, correct inaccuracies and log all identified mistakes. This iteration also involves re-examining the ground truth from the first round to uncover earlier errors.

Additionally, we developed an algorithm to generate synthetic **Aktiva** tables with systematically varied characteristics. This enables experiments investigating these features as potential predictors of extraction performance and allows estimation of an upper bound for extraction accuracy with real **Aktiva** tables.

::: paragraph-start
##### Error Rate Guidance

No separate ground truth exists for the calculated *confidence* scores. We investigate whether true and false predictions can be distinguished based on the returned *confidence scores*. The validity of a prediction is determined using the previously described ground truth datasets.
:::

### Ground Truth Dataset Composition

```{r count-benchmark-documents, echo=echo_flag, warning=warning_flag, message=message_flag, cache=TRUE, cache.extra = tools::md5sum(c("../benchmark_truth/aktiva_passiva_guv_table_pages_no_ocr.csv", "./scripts/page_identification_preparations.R"))}
source("./scripts/page_identification_preparations.R")

num_multiple_tables_per_document <- df_targets_no_ocr %>%
  anti_join(consecutive_pages, by = c("filepath", "page", "type")) %>% 
  arrange(filepath, page) %>%
  group_by(filepath, type) %>% 
  summarise(count = n()) %>% 
  filter(count > 1) %>%
  group_by(filepath) %>% 
  summarise(count = n()) %>% 
  nrow()

multiple_tables_per_type_and_document <- data_unnested %>%
  anti_join(consecutive_pages, by = c("filepath", "page", "type")) %>% 
  arrange(filepath, page) %>%
  group_by(filepath, type) %>% 
  summarise(count = n()) %>% 
  filter(count > 1) %>% 
  group_by(type) %>% 
  summarise("multiple targets in document" = n())

df_special_targets <- multiple_tables_per_type_and_document %>% left_join(consecutive_pages %>% group_by(type) %>% summarise("target two pages long" = n())) %>% mutate_if(is.numeric,coalesce,0)
```

This section details the composition of the resulting ground truth datasets for each task, specifying the number of documents per company and the creation of the synthetic dataset.

Among the `r total_pages_no_ocr` pages, `r num_tables` tables must be identified on `r num_target_pages` pages. ```{r table-extraction-preps, echo=FALSE, warning=warning_flag, message=message_flag, cache=TRUE, cache.extra = tools::md5sum('data_storage/real_table_extraction_llm.rds')}
old_doc_base <- readRDS("data_storage/real_table_extraction_llm.rds") %>% select(filepath) %>% unique()
new_doc_base <- readRDS("data_storage/real_table_extraction_extended_llm.rds") %>% select(filepath) %>% unique() %>% mutate(filepath = str_replace(filepath, "a__f", "af")) %>% filter(!str_detect(filepath, "MEAB GmbH"))
```

::: paragraph-start
##### Information Extraction {#information-extraction-data-sampling}

Transcribing all values from a \acr{PDF} document into a \acr{csv} file can take up to 12 minutes per table, with a maximum of 40 values to copy, format or enter manually. Beyond this manual process, conceptual decisions are sometimes required to match values to the strict schema. Occasionally, values must be omitted if no suitable row exists, or multiple values must be summed to fit the predefined schema.
:::

This manual process is completed for `r old_doc_base %>% nrow()` documents. We include a single **Aktiva** table from each company reporting the balance sheet at the granularity required by our schema. Additional documents from *Amt für Statistik und Brandenburg* are included to assess whether in-context learning improves performance when are used.

Subsequently, \acr{LLM} predictions are used to create an additional `r (new_doc_base %>% nrow())-(old_doc_base %>% nrow())` ground truth tables. The original ground truth tables are reviewed in this iteration, revealing an error rate of 2.4%. Thus, the human reference score for the percentage of correct predictions is 0.976. Figure \@ref(fig:table-extraction-doc-base) shows the number of **Aktiva** tables used for information extraction tasks with real data, as opposed to synthetic data.

```{r table-extraction-doc-base, echo=echo_flag, warning=warning_flag, message=message_flag, out.width="100%", dev=std_dev, fig.cap="Showing the number of documents used for the table extraction task. The number of Aktiva tables is equal to the number documents.", fig.width=9}
new_doc_base %>% rowwise() %>% 
  mutate(
    .before = 1, 
    company = str_match(filepath, "/pvc/benchmark_truth/real_tables_extended/(.*)__")[2],
    initial_doc_base = str_remove(filepath, "_extended") %in% old_doc_base$filepath
    ) %>% ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(x = company, fill = initial_doc_base)) +
  scale_x_discrete(
    guide = guide_axis(angle = 60),
    labels = scales::label_wrap(30)
    ) +
  theme(
    axis.title.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.margin = margin(l = 0)
  )
```

We generate synthetic **Aktiva** tables to address the limited number of real tables and to systematically investigate potential predictors of extraction performance, even when specific table characteristics are unevenly distributed in the real dataset. A detailed description of the systematically varied table features is provided in the Appendix \@ref(synthetic-table-extraction). This process results in 16,504 tables created in three formats each.

## Data Processing

This section outlines the data flow for \acr{LLM} approaches. Figure \@ref(fig:data-flow-llm) visualizes the various processing steps. The blue area depicts the benchmark data flow, beginning with the \acr{PDF} of an annual report as input and ending with \acr{json}-formatted benchmark results as output. The green area illustrates how R is used to visualize results for analysis and interpretation. R Markdown is employed to document the results in this thesis.

```{r data-flow-llm, fig.cap="Showing the processing steps from input data to the results in this thesis.", out.width="100%", echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("images/unified_flowchart.png")
```

We start by extracting the text for each page from the annual reports, using PDF extraction libraries like *pdfium* and *pymupdf*. We do this once for each document and save all text extracts page-wise in a \acr{json} file. We record the original file path and corresponding pagenumber as meta data.

We embed the text extracts in the prompt template — either in the text section at the end or as an example in the blank section (see Figure \@ref(fig:prompt-setup-classification)). The prompt is then processed by the algorithm, predicting, if the text contains a specific type of information or not. The predictions are compared with the ground truth.

The results of this evaluation are saved as \acr{json}. We save the result for every individual evaluation, as well as calculated performance metrics and the runtime needed to process all texts as batch. This allows us to reevaluate or exclude specific results and recalculate the aggregated metrics later. All steps from the text extraction to the result saving are implemented in *Python*.

The process for the information extraction is similar. One difference is, that the algorithm makes multiple predictions per text. Thus, we do not save a single prediction and its evaluation result but a data frame with all predictions and all ground truth values. Saving the ground truth values in this data frame is not necessary but allows us a more convenient reevaluation.

## Evaluation and Reporting

We primarily use *R* for evaluation, visualization, and reporting. The *bookdown* library[^04_implementation-1] is employed to create a report linked to our data, automatically updating figures and tables as new results are added. This enables us to conduct additional experiments until the final stages of thesis writing.

[^04_implementation-1]: For future projects, we will likely use *Quarto* instead of *bookdown*, as it is Posit's new reporting framework, which we discovered too late for this thesis.

Additionally, this approach allows us to produce both \acr{PDF} and \acrfull{HTML} versions of the thesis with minimal extra effort. The HTML version can include interactive elements such as paginated tables with search and sorting capabilities, image lightboxes, and image sliders, presenting extensive information without occupying excessive space. The \acr{HTML} version is also more machine-readable.

## Speedup With vLLM and Batching

Final experiments are conducted using the \acr{vllm} library in Python, leveraging its batch processing capabilities. Initial tests used the *transformers* library directly without batching. The resulting runtime improvements are detailed in the Appendix \@ref(vllm-batch-speed).

## Hardware Normalization {#gpu-benchmark}

To ensure comparability of runtimes for different \acr{LLM}s operating on various types and quantities of \acr{GPU}s, we benchmark Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-32B with different hardware configurations on the Datexis cluster. Figure \@ref(fig:gpu-benchmark-plot) displays the runtime for classifying 100 pages using the multi-class approach with three random examples for in-context learning.

Classification with Qwen2.5-32B on B200 \acr{GPU}s is slightly faster than with Qwen2.5-7B on the same number of A100 \acr{GPU}s. We calculate normalized runtimes for our experiments based on these benchmarks for small and large \acr{LLM}s on different \acr{GPU} types and quantities. One minute of computation on a single B200 is equivalent to 4:30 minutes on a single A100.

```{r gpu-benchmark-plot, echo=echo_flag, warning=warning_flag, message=message_flag, dev=std_dev, fig.cap="Showing the runtime to classify 100 pages with the multi-class approach, providing three random examples for the in-context learning.", fig.height=3}
df_gpu_benchmark <- read_csv("../benchmark_jobs/page_identification/gpu_benchmark/gpu_factors.csv")

df_gpu_benchmark %>% ggplot(aes(x = gpu_number, y = runtime_in_s, color = gpu_type)) + geom_line(aes(linetype = model_name)) + geom_point()
```

## Summary

This chapter documents the choices and steps taken to implement an experimental setup for evaluating the foundation of an automated system for page identification and information extraction in financial documents.

Overall, the implementation effectively translated the proposed methodology into a functional and adaptable system, establishing a basis for subsequent evaluation and practical application.

The following section presents the key results from experiments conducted with this implementation, highlighting the performance of different models and approaches for both page identification and information extraction, and providing insights into their effectiveness and potential areas for improvement.
